target.title: A neural speech decoding framework leveraging deep learning and speech synthesis

read.pdf: Main PDF pp. 1-14: Figs. 1-6 and references (no main-text tables); Reporting Summary pp. 15-17. Supplementary PDF pp. 2-13: Figs. S1-S10 and Table S1.

entries.text: The cohort comprised 48 native English-speaking participants with refractory epilepsy; 26 were female and 22 male.
entries.condition: Clinical ECoG cohort at NYU Langone Hospital; participants performed overt word-production tasks.
entries.quote: We collected neural data from 48 native English-speaking participants (26 female, 22 male) with refractory epilepsy who had ECoG subdural electrode grids implanted at NYU Langone Hospital.

entries.text: Coverage comprised 5 hybrid-density and 43 low-density participants; 32 had left-hemisphere and 16 right-hemisphere implants.
entries.condition: Same 48-person clinical ECoG cohort; hemisphere refers to implant location.
entries.quote: Five participants underwent HB sampling, and 43 LD sampling. The ECoG array was implanted on the left hemisphere for 32 participants and on the right for 16.

entries.text: The five elicitation tasks were auditory repetition, auditory naming, sentence completion, word/visual reading, and picture naming; Methods calls reading VR while Results calls it WR.
entries.condition: Native English-speaking epilepsy participants produced target words to auditory or visual stimuli; the VR/WR naming differs between Methods and Results.
entries.loc: Methods: Experiments design; Results: Data collection

entries.text: The five tasks used 50 repeated unique words and yielded 400 trials per participant, aligned to speech-production onset.
entries.condition: Word-level spoken production across the five auditory/visual tasks; all trials aligned to speech onset.
entries.quote: We provided 50 repeated unique words (400 total trials per participant), all of which were analysed locked to the onset of speech production.

entries.text: Each target word occurred once in auditory naming and sentence completion and twice in each of the other three tasks.
entries.value: 1 in AN/SC; 2 in each other task
entries.condition: Fifty target words distributed across the five tasks for each participant.

entries.text: Mean produced-speech duration was 500 ms per trial.
entries.condition: Overt target-word production during the five elicitation tasks.

entries.text: Methods specify 10 randomly selected test trials from each task, giving 350 training and 50 test trials per participant.
entries.condition: Five tasks and 400 total trials per participant; split is within participant and trial-based.
entries.quote: The decoding models were trained separately for each participant using all trials except ten randomly selected ones from each task, leading to 350 trials for training and 50 for testing.

entries.text: Results separately describe an 80/20 train/test split, which conflicts with Methods' 350/50 allocation out of 400 trials (87.5/12.5%).
entries.condition: Per participant; Results: Data collection versus Methods: Data collection and preprocessing. The stated counts imply 87.5/12.5%, not 80/20%.
entries.quote: We trained a model for each participant using 80% of available data for that participant and evaluated the model on the remaining 20% of data
entries.loc: Results: Data collection; Methods: Data collection and preprocessing

entries.text: A stricter causal-ResNet cross-validation held out 10 unique words entirely from speech-autoencoder pretraining and ECoG-decoder training, using five folds; this tests unseen words, not unseen speakers.
entries.condition: Word-level held-out validation; training and validation folds have non-overlapping words. The paper calls performance comparable to the trial-held-out evaluation but gives no fold-wise point estimates in text.
entries.quote: To ensure our framework can generalize well to unseen words, we added a more stringent word-level cross-validation in which random (ten unique) words were entirely held out during training
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2b

entries.text: The number and timing of recording sessions per participant are not specified; recordings are described as collected during the hospital stay.
entries.condition: Evaluation used within-participant trials; session-level independence or repeated-session generalization cannot be determined from the text.

entries.text: ECoG was sampled at 2,048 Hz and downsampled to 512 Hz before processing.
entries.condition: Per electrode, before high-gamma envelope extraction.

entries.text: A Hilbert transform extracted the high-gamma (70-150 Hz) envelope, which was then downsampled to 125 Hz.
entries.condition: ECoG features supplied to the neural decoder after rereferencing and artifact/epileptiform-channel exclusion.

entries.text: The ECoG reference mean and variance were estimated from a 250-ms silent pre-stimulus period within the training set.
entries.condition: Reference signal averaged across silent periods; electrode signals were normalized to this reference.

entries.text: After common-average rereferencing, each electrode signal was z-scored to its training-set silent-reference mean and variance.
entries.condition: Neural-signal preprocessing; the paper does not describe a separate speech-spectrogram normalization for PCC evaluation.

entries.text: The low-density clinical grid used 64 macro contacts in an 8 x 8 array with 10-mm spacing.
entries.condition: Low-density sampling in 43 participants; clinical subdural ECoG grids.

entries.text: Each hybrid-density array added 64 smaller interspersed electrodes to the 64 macro contacts, for 128 total contacts; micro/macro center spacing was 5 mm.
entries.condition: Hybrid-density arrays in five participants; additional electrodes were interspersed between macro contacts.
entries.loc: Methods: Data collection and preprocessing; Fig. 3b

entries.text: Training is two-stage: speech-only semi-supervised autoencoder pretraining, followed by supervised ECoG-to-speech decoder training using paired neural and acoustic data.
entries.condition: The speech encoder and differentiable synthesizer are pretrained on speech; the ECoG decoder is then trained with neural signals and ground-truth spectrograms.

entries.text: The speech encoder and synthesizer are subject-specific and can be trained from a participant's speech without matching ECoG; these parameters provide guidance during ECoG-decoder training.
entries.condition: Speech-only pretraining; participant-specific encoder and synthesizer parameters.

entries.text: Praat-estimated pitch and four formant frequencies supervise the speech encoder, resampled to the 125-Hz neural/spectrogram rate; spectrogram and STOI losses are also used.
entries.condition: Semi-supervised speech-autoencoder pretraining; Praat labels supplement spectrogram reconstruction and STOI losses.
entries.quote: Specifically, we used the Praat method to estimate the pitch and four formant frequencies

entries.text: The interpretable acoustic latent representation contains 18 speech parameters per time step.
entries.condition: Decoder estimates the parameters from ECoG; the synthesizer maps them to a spectrogram.
entries.quote: In total, the synthesizer input includes 18 speech parameters at each time step.

entries.text: The compared ECoG decoders were 3D ResNet, 3D Swin Transformer, and LSTM; causal and non-causal variants were evaluated.
entries.condition: Same speech-encoder guidance and synthesizer; participant-level held-out trial evaluation.
entries.quote: We provide multiple ECoG decoder architectures to choose from, including 3D ResNet, 3D Swin Transformer and LSTM.

entries.text: Causal models use past and current neural samples; non-causal models also use future samples, which can contain feedback unavailable in real-time use.
entries.condition: Temporal causality of the ECoG decoder; all paper performance comparisons are offline.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality

entries.text: The synthesizer produces spectrograms, then Griffin-Lim inversion produces speech waveforms.
entries.condition: At inference the ECoG decoder and synthesizer are used; the speech encoder is not required.
entries.quote: which are then converted to a waveform by the Griffin–Lim algorithm

entries.text: The authors claim naturalistic speech that closely resembles each speaker's own voice.
entries.condition: Author characterization of synthesized audio; no blinded listener-rating result is reported in the main text.

entries.text: Mean spectrogram PCC was 0.806 for non-causal ResNet and 0.797 for causal ResNet; the authors report no significant difference.
entries.condition: N=48; each point is a participant's average PCC across held-out test trials; 50-word overt-speech task; per-participant model; no language-model decoding.
entries.quote: mean PCC = 0.806 and 0.797 for non-causal and causal, respectively
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Mean spectrogram PCC was 0.792 for non-causal Swin and 0.798 for causal Swin; the authors report no significant difference.
entries.condition: N=48; participant means over held-out test trials; same five-task, 50-word paradigm and participant-specific training as ResNet.
entries.quote: mean PCC = 0.792 and 0.798 for non-causal and causal, respectively
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Mean spectrogram PCC was 0.745 for non-causal LSTM and 0.712 for causal LSTM; causal LSTM was significantly worse than its non-causal counterpart.
entries.condition: N=48; participant means over held-out test trials; five-task, 50-word overt-speech paradigm.
entries.quote: the performance of the causal LSTM model (PCC = 0.712) was significantly inferior to that of its non-causal (PCC = 0.745) version
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Causal versus non-causal ResNet comparison: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank P=0.093.
entries.condition: Paired participant-level decoding comparison on held-out test trials; mean PCC 0.797 causal versus 0.806 non-causal.
entries.quote: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test P = 0.093
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Causal versus non-causal Swin comparison: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank P=0.196.
entries.condition: Paired participant-level decoding comparison on held-out test trials; mean PCC 0.798 causal versus 0.792 non-causal.
entries.quote: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test P = 0.196
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Causal versus non-causal LSTM comparison: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank P=0.009; causal LSTM performed worse.
entries.condition: Paired participant-level decoding comparison on held-out test trials; mean PCC 0.712 causal versus 0.745 non-causal.
entries.quote: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test P = 0.009
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Causal ResNet versus causal Swin comparison: Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank P=0.587; no significant difference was found.
entries.condition: Paired participant-level comparison on held-out test trials; causal mean PCCs 0.797 and 0.798.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2a

entries.text: Mean decoded-versus-reference speech-parameter PCCs were 0.781 for voice weight, 0.571 for loudness, and 0.889 for pitch f0.
entries.unit: mean PCC for voice weight; loudness; pitch f0
entries.condition: Causal ResNet; PCC between decoded and speech-encoder reference parameter time series; reported across participants.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2d-f

entries.text: Mean decoded-versus-reference speech-parameter PCCs were 0.812 for formant f1 and 0.883 for formant f2.
entries.condition: Causal ResNet; decoded versus speech-encoder reference parameter time series; reported across participants.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2f

entries.text: The authors claim generalization to words absent from all training stages and describe performance as comparable to trial-held-out evaluation.
entries.condition: Causal ResNet; five-fold word-level validation with 10 random words excluded from speech-encoder/synthesizer pretraining and ECoG-decoder training.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality; Fig. 2b

entries.text: Right-hemisphere causal decoding yielded PCC 0.790 for ResNet and 0.798 for Swin, with no reported significant difference from left-hemisphere decoding.
entries.condition: Left implants N=32; right implants N=16; causal decoders; participant-level test performance.
entries.loc: Results: Left-hemisphere versus right-hemisphere decoding; Fig. 3a

entries.text: Left-versus-right PCC comparisons gave P=0.623 for ResNet and P=0.968 for Swin.
entries.condition: Independent group comparison of causal model PCCs; left N=32 and right N=16. The Fig. 3 caption labels Swin an independent Wilcoxon test.
entries.loc: Results: Left-hemisphere versus right-hemisphere decoding; Fig. 3a

entries.text: The authors report similar causal decoding performance for hybrid- and low-density grids and no consistent gain from the extra hybrid electrodes.
entries.condition: Hybrid-density N=5; low-density N=43; within-hybrid comparison uses all electrodes versus only low-density electrodes.
entries.loc: Results: Effect of electrode density; Fig. 3c-d

entries.text: For all-electrode versus low-density-in-hybrid PCCs, the five participant P values were 0.114, 0.003, 0.0773, 0.472, and 0.605; the text notes one exception.
entries.condition: Causal ResNet; five hybrid-grid participants; 50 test trials per participant; Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank tests.
entries.quote: There are no statistically significant differences for four out of five participants (Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test, P = 0.114, 0.003, 0.0773, 0.472 and 0.605, respectively).

entries.text: The authors characterize results as similar to or better than many prior reports; participant PCCs span 0.62-0.92, causal-ResNet mean/median are 0.797/0.805, and 54% exceeded 0.8 PCC.
entries.condition: Across participants and several architectures; causal ResNet mean and median are participant-level test performance; N=48.

entries.text: The paper characterizes earlier linear neural-to-spectrogram approaches as achieving PCC about 0.6 or lower; this is a contextual prior-study claim, not a matched benchmark.
entries.condition: Earlier linear models decoding/synthesizing neural speech spectrograms; the paper notes different stimuli and electrode sampling complicate comparison.

entries.text: The authors caution that direct comparison with prior reports is complicated by differing metrics, decoded stimuli, and cortical sampling.
entries.condition: Cross-study comparison of continuous speech versus single words and of high-/low-density or depth/surface electrodes.

entries.text: The authors claim their acoustic intermediate representation is more accurate than direct ECoG-to-spectrogram mapping and ECoG-to-random-vector GAN synthesis.
entries.condition: The direct-spectrogram and GAN comparisons are described in Supplementary Fig. 10 and are based on three hybrid-density participants.
entries.quote: Our intermediate acoustic representation led to significantly more accurate speech decoding than directly mapping ECoG to the speech spectrogram

entries.text: The authors argue explicit acoustic speech parameters preserve speaker-specific characteristics and produce natural-sounding output, unlike kinematic representations.
entries.condition: Claim about the output representation and synthesizer; not an independently rated listener study in the main text.

entries.text: The authors report speech synthesis delay under 50 ms and cite Supplementary Table 1 for the inference-time measurements.
entries.condition: Inference-time claim for neural-to-speech output; main text says real-time decoding was not the study's focus.

entries.text: Supplementary Table 1 reports causal-ResNet total inference times of 43.99 +/- 1.09 ms at N_FFT=256 and 45.97 +/- 0.80 ms at N_FFT=512 on an RTX-3060 GPU.
entries.unit: mean +/- SD ms, total ECoG-to-waveform inference
entries.condition: GPU RTX-3060; causal ResNet; total combines ECoG-to-spectrogram and spectrogram-to-waveform; supplementary table states mean and standard deviation.
entries.quote: Although our current focus was not real-time decoding, we were able to synthesize speech from neural signals with a delay of under 50 ms (Supplementary Table 1)

entries.text: The causal Swin total inference time in Supplementary Table 1 was 59.13 +/- 0.74 ms at N_FFT=256 and 60.87 +/- 0.75 ms at N_FFT=512 on RTX-3060.
entries.unit: mean +/- SD ms, total ECoG-to-waveform inference
entries.condition: GPU RTX-3060; causal 3D Swin; total combines ECoG-to-spectrogram and spectrogram-to-waveform; table also reports LSTM totals of 41.22 +/- 1.19 and 42.77 +/- 1.28 ms for FFT 256/512.
entries.quote: Although our current focus was not real-time decoding, we were able to synthesize speech from neural signals with a delay of under 50 ms (Supplementary Table 1)

entries.text: PCC evaluates decoded-versus-actual speech spectrograms; STOI+ is also used to measure intelligibility. No chance-level baseline is stated.
entries.condition: Held-out test evaluation of spectrogram quality and intelligibility; the text does not provide a null/chance reference for either metric.
entries.quote: We also use STOI+, as described in Methods section Training of the ECoG decoder to measure the intelligibility of the decoded speech.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds or the number of independent model-training repetitions for trial-level or word-level evaluations.
entries.condition: The trial test selection and held-out-word folds are described as random, but seed and repeated-run counts are absent.
entries.quote: The decoding models were trained separately for each participant using all trials except ten randomly selected ones from each task, leading to 350 trials for training and 50 for testing.
entries.loc: Methods: Data collection and preprocessing; Fig. 2b

entries.text: The trial-held-out evaluation is within participant: separate models are trained per participant and held-out trials come from that participant; no held-out-speaker test is reported.
entries.condition: Same participants contribute training and test trials; word identities can recur across tasks and the separate word-level validation is the stated unseen-word analysis.

entries.text: The paper specifies electrode-wise neural z-scoring but does not specify any additional speech-spectrogram normalization used specifically for PCC evaluation.
entries.condition: The stated preprocessing normalizes each ECoG electrode to a silent-reference mean and variance; PCC is described on decoded and actual spectrograms.
entries.loc: Methods: Data collection and preprocessing; Evaluation metrics

entries.text: Speech-autoencoder loss weights were empirically tuned by testing parameter choices on three hybrid-density participants; the exact selection partition and whether it overlapped final test data are not specified.
entries.condition: Speech encoder/synthesizer pretraining; methods give loss weights but do not identify a separate validation set or selection trials.

entries.text: The final model/architecture choice for subsequent analyses is reported after model comparisons, but the paper does not identify a separate validation partition or state whether selection was independent of the test results.
entries.condition: Models were compared on held-out testing data; causal ResNet and Swin were selected for further analyses.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality

entries.text: The authors concede that the ECoG-to-speech decoder requires paired speech and ECoG training data; using imagined/mimed neural signals with older or proxy speech would require a revised alignment strategy.
entries.condition: Current study uses synchronized overt speech and neural recordings; suitability for paralysed participants is proposed rather than demonstrated.

entries.text: The authors concede that 3D ResNet and 3D Swin assume grid-based electrode sampling; strips and depth electrodes such as sEEG require future model development.
entries.condition: Current neural decoder architecture is designed for grid-shaped ECoG arrays.

entries.text: The authors concede this is word-level decoding limited to a 50-word vocabulary and may not be directly comparable to sentence-level decoding.
entries.condition: Overt isolated target-word production; comparisons to continuous or sentence-level speech are not matched.

entries.text: The right-hemisphere finding is feasibility evidence from participants with intact left-hemisphere coverage, not a demonstration in people with left-hemisphere damage; the authors say that population must be tested.
entries.condition: Right-hemisphere decoding was evaluated in the existing epilepsy cohort; no participant with left-hemisphere damage is described.

entries.text: Although causal models are presented as suitable for real-time prostheses, the authors explicitly say real-time decoding was not the study's focus; no closed-loop use-time session is reported.
entries.condition: Offline causal model evaluations and inference-time measurement; speech was generated from overt word-production recordings.

entries.text: Only one participant's neural and audio data are publicly downloadable; access to other participants' audio is restricted to approved research requests because of sensitivity and consent limits.
entries.unit: participant with public neural and audio data
entries.condition: The full 48-participant cohort is not publicly available as unrestricted neural-plus-audio data.

entries.text: No user confirmation or accept/reject step between decoded speech generation and output is described.
entries.condition: The described pipeline produces the decoded speech waveform directly; user-facing confirmation behavior is not reported.

entries.text: No user correction, editing, or post-decoding repair interaction is described.
entries.condition: The paper evaluates reconstruction of speech parameters and spectrograms, not an interactive correction loop.

entries.text: In the v1.0.1 HDF5 loader, training samples are drawn from valid-index rows before the configured test suffix, while test mode indexes the final TestNum rows; the shipped NY742 example config sets 10 per each of five tasks.
entries.value: 10 per task in shipped example config
entries.condition: This is the repository implementation/example configuration; paper text describes randomly selected test trials, and the released HDF5 ordering/pre-shuffling semantics are not documented here.

entries.text: The v1.0.1 training loader randomly chooses training events and a temporal crop offset from -64 to speech-end minus 64 samples; test crops start at speech onset minus the configured test lead.
entries.condition: Random event/crop sampling is in addition to the paper's stated trial split; test alignment is fixed by ahead_onset_test.

entries.text: The v1.0.1 loader accepts seed=None, uses NumPy random sampling, and the training script shows no explicit RNG seeding; exact reproducibility seeds are not provided in the code path reviewed.
entries.condition: Random train-event and crop selection; the paper also omits RNG seeds and independent rerun counts.
entries.quote: The code is available at https://github.com/flinkerlab/neural_speech_decoding (10.5281/zenodo.10719428).

entries.text: The released ECoG-to-speech script evaluates the held-out test dataset after each training epoch and saves test samples/checkpoints every 10 epochs; it defines no separate validation dataset in this loop.
entries.condition: Code behavior in v1.0.1; the paper does not describe this evaluation cadence or a distinct validation split.
entries.quote: The code is available at https://github.com/flinkerlab/neural_speech_decoding (10.5281/zenodo.10719428).

entries.text: The v1.0.1 example config sets ahead_onset to 32 frames for train and test; the loader starts test crops at onset minus that configured lead.
entries.condition: Example production config has DOWN_TF_FS and DOWN_ECOG_FS both 125 Hz; paper states onset-locked analysis but not this exact crop lead.

entries.text: Supplementary contamination analysis reports P=0.77 for an example participant and uses 10,000 shuffled contamination matrices; analysis was also conducted across all 48 participants.
entries.condition: Acoustic-contamination check comparing audio and neural frequency-component correlations; the supplementary figure names the example participant LD43.
entries.loc: Methods: Data collection and preprocessing; Supplementary Fig. 5

entries.text: Supplementary Fig. S3 gives STOI+ P values 0.626, 0.146, 0.881, 0.058, and 0.414 for all-electrode versus low-density-in-hybrid comparisons across five participants.
entries.condition: Causal ResNet; five hybrid-density participants; 50 test trials per participant; Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test.
entries.quote: the decoding results were not significantly different from each other (with the exception of participant 2) in terms of PCC and STOI+
entries.loc: Results: Effect of electrode density; Supplementary Fig. S3

entries.text: The authors state ResNet achieved the highest mean PCC across the 48 participants; Swin followed closely and LSTM was consistently lower.
entries.condition: Comparison across non-causal and causal ResNet, Swin, and LSTM on participant-level held-out test performance.
entries.loc: Results: Speech decoding performance and causality

entries.text: The authors call the ECoG-to-speech framework novel and emphasize its low-dimensional acoustic representation guided by speech-only, subject-specific pretraining.
entries.condition: Speech encoder and synthesizer are trained subject-specifically on speech; the ECoG decoder maps neural signals to interpretable acoustic parameters.

entries.text: The authors present unseen-word generalization as an advantage over pattern-matching approaches that produce subject-specific utterances but generalize poorly.
entries.condition: Claim based on the five-fold word-level validation; not a sentence-level or held-out-speaker test.

entries.text: The authors claim causal convolutional and transformer models perform on par with non-causal counterparts while recruiting more relevant cortical structures for real-time decoding.
entries.condition: Causal ResNet and Swin; cortical contribution inferred from occlusion maps; real-time closed-loop use was not evaluated.

entries.text: No external lexical language model, phoneme-transition rescoring, or language-model correction at inference is described; the system is presented as acoustic-parameter decoding followed by synthesis.
entries.condition: The speech encoder is a training-time guide and is not needed after training; no inference-time linguistic aid is specified.

entries.text: For the reported loss-weight tuning on three hybrid-density participants, the paper does not specify the trial split, validation metric, or whether final evaluation trials were excluded from tuning.
entries.condition: Speech-autoencoder and ECoG-decoder loss weights were empirically selected; exact selection data are not identified.

entries.text: Main Results reports subject-specific 8x8 ECoG-grid spectrogram PCC of 0.817 across 43 participants.
entries.condition: Within-participant (subject-specific); low-density 8x8 ECoG grid only; N=43; Main Results value.
entries.quote: The subject-specific models using only low-density 8x8 ECoG data achieved high decoding Pearson Correlation Coefficient with ground truth spectrogram (PCC=0.817), over N=43 participants

entries.text: Detailed Figure 3 results report subject-specific SwinTW PCC of 0.825 for 64-electrode ECoG-grid models.
entries.condition: Within-participant; 64 electrodes on one 8x8 ECoG grid; N=43; detailed Results value, distinct from the Main Results value.
entries.loc: Results, Subject-Specific Models: Speech Decoding with Electrodes on One ECoG Grid (Figure 3)

entries.text: Subject-specific models using additional selected electrodes report PCC 0.838 in 39 participants.
entries.condition: Within-participant; 8x8 ECoG grid plus additional strip, depth, and grid electrodes; N=39.
entries.loc: Main Results; Results, Subject-Specific Models: Speech Decoding with Additional Electrodes (Figure 4)

entries.text: The SwinTW decoding is non-causal by architectural inference: temporal attention is described without a causal restriction or causal mask.
entries.value: non-causal (inferred from the described temporal attention; no causal mask is reported)
entries.condition: The paper describes temporal self-attention in windows but does not explicitly label this decoder causal or non-causal.
entries.quote: We still have spatial and temporal attention, but windowing is only applied in the temporal direction to constrain temporal attention.
entries.loc: Method, Neural Decoder based on Temporal Swin Transformer: Temporal window attention

entries.text: Unseen-participant multi-subject spectrogram PCC is 0.765 on average.
entries.condition: Participants outside the training set; Main Results calls this leave-one-out cross-validation, while the detailed Results describes 5-fold cross-validation separately for male and female participants.
entries.quote: The multi-subject models achieved high performance on unseen participants, with an average PCC=0.765 in leave-one-out cross-validation.
entries.loc: Main Results; Results, Multi-Subject Model: Evaluation on Participants Outside the Training Set (Figure 6)

entries.text: Five word-production paradigms used a shared vocabulary of 50 target words: Auditory Repetition, Auditory Naming, Sentence Completion, Visual Reading, and Picture Naming.
entries.value: 50 shared target words across five tasks
entries.condition: The five tasks yielded 400 recorded trials per participant.
entries.quote: Each task included the same 50 target words

entries.text: The per-participant split was 350 training trials and 50 held-out test trials, with 10 test trials randomly selected per task.
entries.value: 350 train / 50 test trials; 10 test trials per task
entries.condition: Split from 400 trials across the five word-production tasks.
entries.quote: 350 trials were used for model training, and 50 trials were held out for testing (10 randomly selected trials were reserved for testing for each task).

entries.text: The two-stage decoder maps cortical activity to articulatory movement representations before mapping those representations to speech acoustics.
entries.value: cortical activity → articulatory movement representations → speech acoustics
entries.condition: Recurrent neural network decoder with an articulatory intermediate representation.

entries.text: Acoustic features are converted to a waveform with the Mel-log spectral approximation algorithm with mixed excitation in Festvox.
entries.value: Mel-log spectral approximation algorithm with mixed excitation (Festvox)
entries.condition: Applied to acoustic-feature estimates from the neural decoder.

entries.text: The DenseNet regresses a logarithmic mel-scaled spectrogram (logMel) from ECoG activity.
entries.condition: Intermediate acoustic target predicted from speech-production-area ECoG.

entries.text: A Wavenet vocoder turns the predicted acoustic representation into an audible waveform.
entries.condition: Waveform synthesis from predicted logMel features.
entries.loc: Abstract, Main Results; Section 2.3, Decoding Approach

entries.text: The study recorded six participants.
entries.condition: Native English-speaking participants with ECoG recordings.

entries.text: Training and testing used participant-specific 5-fold cross-validation.
entries.condition: Disjoint training and test data for each participant.

entries.text: Twenty percent of the training data were reserved as a separate validation set.
entries.condition: Used to analyze network optimization during training.

entries.text: Guenther et al. decoded continuous auditory (formant) parameters that drove a real-time speech synthesizer from motor-cortex activity.

entries.text: Lip2AudSpec trains a lip-video network to predict the bottleneck features of a speech autoencoder of the auditory spectrogram.

questions.q: What exactly is held out in the main test and the unseen-word evaluation, and is generalization tested across speakers?
questions.answer: The reported primary evaluation is trial-held-out within each participant, with 10 trials per task described as test data; a separate five-fold causal-ResNet analysis excludes 10 words from training and pretraining. The paper's Results 80/20 split conflicts with the Methods 350/50 counts. No held-out-speaker evaluation is described, and the number of recording sessions is unstated.

questions.q: Does causal decoding preserve the reported spectrogram accuracy relative to non-causal decoding?
questions.answer: Causal ResNet and Swin means are close to their non-causal counterparts (0.797 vs 0.806 and 0.798 vs 0.792 PCC; P=0.093 and P=0.196). Causal LSTM is lower (0.712 vs 0.745; P=0.009). Causal ResNet and Swin do not significantly differ (P=0.587).

questions.q: What is the evidence for right-hemisphere decoding as a clinical route for left-hemisphere damage?
questions.answer: The cohort shows comparable causal-model PCCs for left- and right-hemisphere implants, but these are data from the existing epilepsy cohort, not participants with left-hemisphere damage. The authors explicitly say that right-hemisphere recordings in that population are needed to verify acceptable decoding.

questions.q: Does the study establish real-time prosthesis performance across the tested architectures?
questions.answer: It reports under-50-ms synthesis delay and RTX-3060 inference measurements, including causal ResNet totals below 50 ms; causal Swin totals exceed 50 ms. The authors state that real-time decoding was not the study's focus, and no closed-loop use-time session is reported.

questions.q: What are the principal scope limitations for claims of natural speech decoding and deployment?
questions.answer: Training requires paired speech and ECoG; the current decoder assumes grid sampling; evaluation is overt word production with a 50-word vocabulary; and right-hemisphere feasibility in left-hemisphere-damaged patients remains untested. Only one participant's neural-plus-audio data are publicly downloadable.

questions.q: Which reproducibility and evaluation conditions remain unspecified or code-only?
questions.answer: The paper does not report RNG seeds, independent training repetitions, a chance-level baseline, session counts, or an independent model-selection partition. The v1.0.1 code reveals suffix-based test indexing, randomized training crops without an explicit seed, test evaluation after each epoch, and a 32-frame onset lead in the example config.
